The struggle for control of Yemen continued in the name of Christianity and Judaism into the sixth century.

At that point, Dhū Nuwās, king of Ḥimyar, began persecuting Christians and seizing their property and wealth. The Abyssinians used this as a reason for military intervention in Yemen in 525 CE. They defeated Dhū Nuwās’s army, and he killed himself by riding his horse into the sea and drowning.
This brought the last Jewish political authority in Yemen to an end, although Judaism itself remained deeply rooted there.
The Jews of Yemen are known to have been Arabs by origin who adopted Judaism as a result of this earlier political history. This is why they spoke Arabic rather than Hebrew.
With their victory, the Abyssinians achieved one of their main goals: the occupation of Yemen and control of the great trade route known since ancient times as the “Incense Route.”
But their ambitions did not end there.
Toward the end of the sixth century, under Abraha al-Ashram, their governor in Yemen, they sought to occupy Mecca, which had by then become the most important commercial centre in the region.
Abraha personally led a military expedition against Mecca and used elephants for transport. For this reason, the Arabs called the year of the Abyssinian attack the “Year of the Elephant.”
But as Abraha’s army reached the approaches to Mecca, it was suddenly struck by an outbreak of smallpox that caused terrible losses. Abraha returned to Sanaa defeated.
Islamic historians generally hold that the Year of the Elephant was also the year in which Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib, the future prophet of Islam, was born.
The Abyssinian campaign against Mecca was therefore one more episode in the struggle for political control, rooted above all in economic interests.
Yet Muslim chroniclers usually explain it in purely religious terms.
The Abyssinians’ defeat led the conflict to enter a new stage involving new powers.

Khosrow Anūshirwān (531–578 CE), the Persian king at the time, took advantage of the weakness that the Abyssinians suffered in Yemen after this defeat. He moved to seize the opportunity and establish Persian control over this strategic part of the peninsula.

His aim was helped by the fact that the Arabs of Yemen had already rebelled against Abyssinian rule under the leadership of Sayf ibn Dhī Yazan. The Yemeni leader appealed to Khosrow Anūshirwān for help.
Khosrow immediately took advantage of the situation. He assembled an army and sent it across the “Persian” Gulf to Yemen.

The result was that the Abyssinian occupiers were driven out, only to be replaced by Persian occupiers. Persian rule continued until the rise of Islam, when the Muslims expelled the Persians and Yemen once again became an Arab-Islamic territory.
Christianity and Judaism therefore competed in this part of the Arabian Peninsula in the service of political ambitions expressed in religious terms.
But this describes only one side of the Jewish-Christian presence in pre-Islamic Arabia. There was another side as well, connected with the development of religious thought.

The presence of these two religions helped change religious awareness in the peninsula by encouraging a more abstract way of thinking about existence, one that moved beyond the simple, sensory outlook of pagan religion.

Pagan ideas and Jewish and Christian ideas about the existence of the world had lived side by side for a long time. It was therefore natural for them to influence one another and for debates to spread about creation, God, the nature of God, resurrection, the Last Judgment, and prophecy.
Over time, this long interaction left its mark on people’s thinking.

Eventually, a group appeared within pre-Islamic society whose position on these great questions of existence differed from all three established religious positions. They were neither pagan nor Jewish nor Christian. Instead, they developed a distinct and reflective outlook.
This was a sign that something new was beginning to emerge from within the old order itself.

Such a group did in fact appear during the final period before Islam. It emerged from among those whom pre-Islamic society knew as “sages.” Its members rejected idol worship and the belief in many gods and called instead for belief in one God, but without adopting the specifically Jewish or Christian approach to religion.
These were the people known as the Ḥunafāʾ, or Aḥnāf.
We have already referred several times in this chapter to what we called the phenomenon of the Ḥunafāʾ shortly before Islam.
Who were these people? Why were they called Ḥunafāʾ? What exactly did they believe? Did they add a new religion to those already found among the pre-Islamic Arabs?
Arab chroniclers and Muslim commentators give the following names as members of this group:

Quss ibn Sāʿida al-Iyādī, Zayd ibn ʿAmr ibn Nufayl, Umayya ibn Abī al-Ṣalt, Arbāb ibn Riʾāb, Suwayd ibn ʿĀmir al-Muṣṭaliqī, Asʿad Abū Karib al-Ḥimyarī, Wakīʿ ibn Salama ibn Zuhayr al-Iyādī, ʿUmayr ibn Jundab al-Juhanī, ʿAdī ibn Zayd al-ʿIbādī, Abū Qays Ṣirma ibn Abī Anas, Sayf ibn Dhī Yazan, Waraqa ibn Nawfal al-Qurashī, ʿĀmir ibn al-Ẓarib al-ʿAdwānī, ʿAbd al-Ṭābikha ibn Thaʿlaba ibn Wabara ibn Quḍāʿa, ʿAllāf ibn Shihāb al-Tamīmī, al-Mutalammis ibn Umayya al-Kinānī, Zuhayr ibn Abī Sulmā, Khālid ibn Sinān ibn Ghayth al-ʿAbsī, ʿAbd Allāh al-Quḍāʿī, ʿUbayd ibn al-Abraṣ al-Asadī, and Kaʿb ibn Luʾayy ibn Ghālib.
According to the Arab chroniclers, most of these people lived during the final years before Islam, while some also lived into the first years of the Islamic period.

Yet those same chroniclers say that some of them became Christians, including ʿAdī ibn Zayd al-ʿIbādī and Arāb ibn Riʾāb. They also claim that others lived centuries before the final pre-Islamic period.

Their accounts of the beliefs of these individuals also show that they did not all hold exactly the same opinions. Nor were they linked together or in regular contact. In other words, they did not form an organized group united by a common movement or shared activity.

This means that the only thing clearly shared by all these “Ḥunafāʾ” was one broad principle. Independently of one another, and often without even knowing one another, they rejected idol worship and belief in many gods and accepted the existence of one God.
Beyond that, the chroniclers give us no clear picture of what they believed, either collectively or individually.
There is, however, one other subject the sources discuss besides this general religious principle: their way of life and moral conduct.

The chroniclers tell us that these Ḥunafāʾ “kept away from other people; some wandered through the land searching for the ḥanīf religion of Abraham; some had read and understood the revealed scriptures; they reflected on the universe; they avoided wine and shameful acts; and they advised people to stay away from idols and draw closer to God.”

But we do not know how they could have “kept away from other people” while at the same time wandering through the land in search of the religion of Abraham. Where would the religion of Abraham have been found if not among people and within human society?

What we can still take from these reports is that some of the “sages” of the pre-Islamic period were looking for a way of understanding the world that differed both from paganism and from Judaism and Christianity.
They reflected on the universe and tried to follow a moral way of life that matched their intellectual convictions.

As for the name Ḥunafāʾ, the writings of Arab chroniclers and the research of Orientalists suggest that the term was already known among the Arabs before Islam and was used for this particular group of sages.

The term appears, both in the singular and the plural, in many Qur’anic verses. These passages suggest that the existence of the Ḥunafāʾ before Islam was taken for granted. They also indicate that the basic meaning of the term, as applied to the group’s religious position, involved two things: first, a complete rejection of paganism; and second, a departure from established Jewish and Christian beliefs.

A scientific historical approach to the question of the Ḥunafāʾ does not need to depend on the exact individuals named by the chroniclers, whose lists are often confused and inconsistent. Nor does it depend on which of those figures supposedly became Christian, or which are said to have lived long before the final pre-Islamic period.

The same applies to doubts about whether some of the people listed among the Ḥunafāʾ even existed as described. Quss ibn Sāʿida is one example. There are also doubts about poems and other sayings attributed to figures such as Umayya ibn Abī al-Ṣalt.
The scientific question does not depend on resolving every one of these disputed details.
What matters is not whether this or that named person really belonged to the Ḥunafāʾ, or whether a particular saying was truly his.
It might even be proved that none of the specific people listed by the chroniclers actually belonged to this group. The larger historical question would still remain.
That question is the appearance, during this particular period shortly before Islam, of a distinct religious current known as the Ḥunafāʾ.
The chroniclers may have confused the names. They may wrongly have called some of these individuals Ḥunafāʾ. They may have attributed sayings to them that they never uttered.

But it is much harder to believe that the chroniclers simply invented, without any basis in historical reality, the existence of the group itself—a group that represented a current, or a phenomenon, of social change taking place within religious consciousness during the final pre-Islamic period.
The essential historical question is the appearance of this current at precisely that time.
There is little reason to think that Muslim storytellers and chroniclers simply invented it.

One indication is that later scholars, especially Orientalists, do not seem to have seriously entertained that possibility—even those who regularly doubted or challenged almost everything Muslim writers recorded about the history of the Arabs before Islam.
On the contrary, the Orientalists who studied the Ḥunafāʾ generally took their historical existence in the pre-Islamic period for granted.

Some therefore concentrated on the origin of the word ḥanīf and tried to discover where the pre-Islamic Arabs had taken the term from when they used it for those who called for belief in one God shortly before Islam.
Others tried to prove that the pre-Islamic Ḥunafāʾ were actually a group of Arab Christian ascetics.
The historical evidence, then, does not deny that this phenomenon existed. It supports it.
But even if we had no such written evidence, the logic of history itself would still require us to recognize the phenomenon.
The rise of the Ḥunafāʾ was a natural result of the changes taking place in sixth-century pre-Islamic society, especially in its economic and social relations.
There was also the factor mentioned earlier: the long interaction, within religious consciousness, between pagan views of the world and Jewish-Christian ones.
We should neither ignore this factor nor underestimate its role in producing a phenomenon such as the Ḥunafāʾ.

But even this religious interaction—how deeply it affected people, how quickly its influence spread, and the direction that influence took—was itself shaped, ultimately, by the decisive development of economic and social relations.
Those material changes helped determine the direction taken by changes in other areas of human consciousness, even when the connection worked through indirect and largely invisible mechanisms.

We have already seen that, toward the end of the pre-Islamic period, social development was beginning to break apart the fragmented tribal framework and move toward a broader form of unity capable of containing new and more developed social conflicts.
Signs of this movement could already be seen in many parts of pre-Islamic life and at different levels.

First, tribal relations were beginning to move toward large alliances between groups of tribes, instead of remaining divided into small isolated units, each tribe fragmented further into clans and sub-clans.
These larger alliances necessarily meant that something deeper was changing in the old idea of narrow, closed tribal independence.
Previously, every tribal unit, however small, had strongly defended its separate independence in order to preserve its internal cohesion and the purity of its own traditions.
Once those same units began entering wider alliances that brought together many tribes and clans, they were giving up part of the old meaning of “independence.”
That, in turn, was one sign of the rapid breakdown of the primitive tribal system.
Second, two major events occurred in the peninsula within a relatively short period before the rise of Islam.

The first was the political conflict in Yemen. After Abraha’s failed Abyssinian campaign against Mecca, this conflict acquired a new historical meaning. It became a struggle between local forces within Yemen and outside powers that either already occupied the country, as the Abyssinians did, or hoped to occupy it, as the Persians did.

The conflict, together with the events leading up to it and the results that followed, created an objective basis for a shared sense that the traditional system of tribal relations had to be reconsidered.
That old system rested on fragmentation: separate, closed, neighbouring tribal units, each existing largely on its own.

The need to rethink those relations began to appear in greater cooperation in the face of external dangers. Most of the peninsula’s inhabitants increasingly had reason to fear that those dangers could eventually reach them as well unless they found a new form of social organization capable of resisting them.

The struggle between the Persian and Roman empires for direct control over the peninsula’s strategically important areas grew more intense after Persia took Yemen from the Abyssinians. The danger that foreign conquest might spread into new parts of Arabia therefore became increasingly clear.
The second major event was the famous Battle of Dhū Qār in 609 CE.

This battle was the clearest expression of that shared feeling that a new kind of relationship was needed among the different tribes of the peninsula, especially those living near the frontier zones of the two competing empires, Persia and Rome.
Some modern writers describe this shared feeling as a form of “national consciousness.”
In the modern scientific sense of the term, this description is historically premature. Even so, it is not entirely removed from the reality of the period.
The Battle of Dhū Qār expressed more than the shared feeling just described.
It also showed that the many different changes taking place throughout the peninsula before Islam were beginning to move in a common direction.

If the report is true that Muḥammad, the future prophet of Islam, witnessed the battle and later said of Dhū Qār, “This was the first day on which the Arabs gained redress against the non-Arabs, and through me they were victorious,” then his use of the terms “Arabs” and “non-Arabs” for the two sides gives the battle an almost decisive historical meaning.
That meaning came from the nature of the changes then taking place throughout the region.

The general movement of events was beginning to produce, in embryonic form, an Arab society in a qualitative sense, rather than simply the quantitative collection of separate tribal groups that had made up “pre-Islamic society.”
What, after all, had pre-Islamic “society” been if not the numerical sum of separate tribal units?

And even if we assume that Muḥammad himself never said, “This was the first day on which the Arabs gained redress against the non-Arabs,” and that the saying actually came from another Arab of the same period, the point would remain.

The statement itself, made around the time of the battle, would still show that the victorious side at Dhū Qār was beginning to be understood as “the Arabs,” rather than simply as a collection of tribes that had gathered together to confront the “non-Arabs.”

It would also suggest that when Islam later gave the peninsula a means of unification, it did so at a particular historical moment because the peninsula’s need for unity had itself become historically mature.
It was within this historical setting that the phenomenon of the Ḥunafāʾ appeared at the level of religious consciousness.
At that level, the Ḥunafāʾ represented another mature expression of the same wider transformation.
But to understand this properly, we should also look at several religious developments that came before the Ḥunafāʾ or appeared alongside them.
These developments took place within pagan religion itself. They can be seen as streams flowing into the broader historical movement toward unity during the final period before Islam.
We find them in a number of developments.
First, groups of tribes began sharing the worship of the same idol.

For example, the tribes of Khathʿam, Bajīla, Bāhila, Daws, Azd al-Sarāt, Hawāzin, al-Ḥārith ibn Kaʿb, Jurm, Zubayd, al-Ghawth ibn Murr ibn Udd, and Banū Hilāl ibn ʿĀmir all worshipped the idol known as Dhū al-Khalaṣa.
Similarly, the tribes of Quḍāʿa, Lakhm, Judhām, ʿĀmila, and Ghaṭafān all worshipped the idol known as al-Uqayṣir.
Second, a practical system had developed for organizing the pagan pilgrimage seasons in Mecca.

Different responsibilities were divided among the economically and religiously powerful Meccan leaders. These included feeding pilgrims, guarding the Kaaba, supplying water, and carrying out other practical duties connected with the pilgrimage.
